title: Historical Truth Is an Odyssey
author: Mario Trabucco della Torretta
summary: In this counterpoint essay for Classical Wisdom, classical archaeologist Mario Trabucco della Torretta opens the long-running Parthenon Marbles debate by examining Homer's Odysseus as literature's founding unreliable narrator, then extends that framework to Lord Byron's own account of confronting Lord Elgin over the Marbles' removal from Athens. He argues that Odysseus's tale to the Phaeacians survives specifically because none was left to bear him witness—no independent corroboration existed to check his account—and that ancient critics like Juvenal and Lucian recognized this rhetorical vulnerability even in antiquity. Trabucco della Torretta then pivots to argue that Byron, routinely cast as history's disinterested moral witness against Elgin, occupies a structurally similar position: a compelling narrator whose testimony does not survive contact with the fuller historical record or his own contradictory statements. The essay, published alongside an editor's note from Classical Wisdom founder Anya Leonard explaining the decision to run a dissenting view after a previous pro-restitution piece, uses classical rhetorical analysis as a tool to interrogate a live cultural-heritage controversy, making the case that persuasive narration and historical truth are not the same thing.
points: The essay uses Homer's Odysseus, read through the ancient critics Juvenal and Lucian, as a case study in how a narrator's unchecked, uncorroborated testimony can pass as truth simply because no one is left to contradict it.

Trabucco della Torretta extends that same skeptical lens to Lord Byron's canonical role as chief witness against Lord Elgin, arguing Byron's own words and the fuller historical record complicate the disinterested moral witness framing.

Classical Wisdom's editorial framing, an editor's note explicitly inviting a dissenting view after a prior pro-restitution piece, makes the essay as much about the ethics of persuasion and disagreement as about the Marbles themselves.

The piece models a distinctly classical-education move: using primary ancient texts (Homer, Juvenal, Lucian) as interpretive tools for a live twenty-first-century cultural argument rather than treating them as merely historical curiosities.
quotes: Odysseus is not merely the founding hero of Western literature. He is its founding unreliable narrator. And the particular form of his unreliability turns out to illuminate, with uncomfortable precision, two centuries of the most consequential cultural argument in the modern world.

Homer signals as much at the very outset: the hero's crew was destroyed, he tells us, because they heedlessly devoured the sun-god's cattle. But that is strikingly different from what Odysseus says happened. The two accounts contradict each other, and Homer's comes first.

Juvenal, writing in the early second century AD, identified the mechanism precisely: Odysseus stirred his listeners to anger and laughter alike as a mendax aretalogus, a lying virtue-signaller, to use a translation our own age might find disconcertingly contemporary, before naming the decisive reason he could get away with it.
The Ithacan's tale was all his own, with none to bear him witness. No surviving companions, no contradicting testimony, no check on the account except the credulity of his hosts.

Lord Byron, poet, philhellene, and the most eloquent prosecutor of Lord Elgin ever to take the stand, is routinely invoked as a kind of disinterested moral witness: the conscience of the age, catching a Scottish earl red-handed on the Acropolis.

Classical Wisdom has previously published arguments in favor of their return. But an intellectual conversation is richer when we are willing to seriously consider arguments with which we may disagree.
